name: Modified GRF (1-29)

lead: Modified GRF (1-29), also called Mod GRF or CJC-1295 without DAC, is a lab-made fragment of GHRH tweaked to resist breakdown. Users pair it with a growth hormone-releasing peptide to get short pulses of growth hormone, aiming for better sleep and recovery, more muscle and a leaner look.

It stimulates GHRH receptors on pituitary cells, releasing growth hormone in a brief pulse. Hormone studies describe the two peptide types working together to release more growth hormone than either alone. No clinical trial cited has tested it for appearance, and user reports are anecdotal and mixed.

paras: Forum users describe it as the GHRH half of a pairing with GHRP-2, GHRP-6 or ipamorelin. Because it is short-acting, it is used to mimic natural pulses of growth hormone, with users reporting sleep, recovery and body-composition changes over weeks.

It is unapproved and listed as prohibited in sport. A Danish forensic analysis of seized powders found products sold as modified GRF (1-29) contained analogues with an extra glycine added, so what is sold online can differ from the label.

angle.text: Mod GRF (CJC-1295 without DAC) is paired with a GH-releasing peptide to give short growth hormone pulses, with users citing better sleep, recovery and a leaner, more muscular look. The pairing's synergy is described in hormone studies; human trials for appearance have not been run.

lead: Modified GRF (1-29), also called Mod GRF, tetrasubstituted GRF (1-29) and CJC-1295 without DAC, is a synthetic 29-amino-acid analogue of the active fragment of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). Four amino acid substitutions are described as making it more resistant to enzymatic breakdown than the natural sequence. [1] It has not been approved as a medicine.

In bodybuilding and peptide forums it is typically described as the GHRH component of a pairing with a growth hormone-releasing peptide (GHRP) such as GHRP-2, GHRP-6 or ipamorelin, with users reporting that the two together release more growth hormone than either alone. [2][3][4][5][6][7]

No published clinical trial cited here has tested Modified GRF (1-29) for muscle, fat loss or appearance. A Danish forensic study of seized doping powders found that products sold as modified GRF (1-29) and other secretagogues contained analogues with an extra glycine added, showing that the material sold online can differ from the labelled compound. [8]
infobox: Mod GRF 1-29, tetrasubstituted GRF(1-29), CJC-1295 no DAC
Not approved; prohibited in sport under WADA rules (per AI-generated encyclopedia text)

paras: Modified GRF (1-29) corresponds to the first 29 residues of the 44-residue human GHRH, the part responsible for receptor binding, with substitutions at positions 2, 8, 15 and 27. [1] An AI-generated encyclopedia entry states that these changes protect it from cleavage by dipeptidyl peptidase-IV and that it was developed in the early 2000s by ConjuChem Biotechnologies; this account has not been verified against primary papers here. [1]

It is distinguished from CJC-1295 with DAC, which carries an additional attachment designed to bind albumin and prolong its action; the version without DAC is described as short-acting. [1] An earlier patent family from 1992 describes amino-terminal-modified GRF analogues with superior activity and potency compared to native GRF, illustrating the longer research history of this class. [9]

No studies found. No human trial of Modified GRF (1-29) for appearance, muscle or fat loss was identified. Related published material concerns chemistry and forensic detection rather than clinical effects, such as the 2019 report of glycine-modified secretagogue analogues, including modified GRF (1-29), in seized material. [8]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, Modified GRF (1-29) is discussed from around 2009 onward as the preferred GHRH analogue among those then available, usually paired with GHRP-2 or GHRP-6. [3][5][2] Users describe taking GHRP-plus-GRF combinations at different times of day, sometimes alongside testosterone, trenbolone or other peptides in logged cycles. [4][5][7][8][10]

Reports of results are mixed in tone. One user who finished a roughly 40-day run of GHRP-2 and Modified GRF said they could not tell whether it worked and described feeling unwell after doses, while another reports improved sleep quality after several months. [2][5]

The sources cited here give no controlled safety data for healthy users. The seized-material study notes that the powders analysed carried an extra glycine at the N-terminus, so that analytical methods for secretagogues needed updating, which indicates variability between labelled and actual content. [8]
The AI-generated encyclopedia text states it is unapproved by regulators such as the FDA and prohibited in sport by WADA. [1]
